chapter: Return in 1965, pay and Preservation Hall
title: Impressions of Preservation Hall in 1965
summary: Wood was glad the musicians were paid but felt the music grandstanded for audiences and still does not like Preservation Hall much.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You know, I always thought that was sort of pitiful that they didn't get paid more for their work. And that when I did come back for my graduation, by that time Preservation Hall was going, and I had never been down there, so I went down to hear that. And I had really real mixed feelings at that time about the whole thing. I liked the idea that the musicians were there and could get a payday and get paid and have an audience, but I also thought that the music had deteriorated something awful, that it was... And again, maybe that was the fact that I had not had a lot of familiarity with them playing, sort of sitting down with a piano in a concert setting as opposed to playing in the streets with a brass band. But I thought it had gotten that they grandstanded for the audience right much and that the music had suffered in the process. Whether that was just some sort of prejudice bond of nostalgia on my part, I really don't know, but I was disappointed in it. And I still really don't like Preservation Hall that much, I think.
